TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
MONDAY, 6 MARCH 2023 AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
DAY 42
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR BORA KAPLAN, for the Commonwealth
MS PHILLIPA KELLY, for the Commonwealth
MR JONATHAN HORTON KC, for The Hon Malcolm Turnbull
MR PHILLIP SHARP, for The Hon Malcolm Turnbull
MR NICHOLAS ANDREATIDIS KC, for Mr Jason McNamara
MS KATE SLACK, for Mr Jason McNamara

COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Thank you, Commissioner. This morning I appear at least in respect of
the first witness with Ms Berry.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, today I appear with Mr Kaplan and Ms Kelly for the
Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. And we have also got - - -
MR HORTON: My name is Horton, initials J.M., appearing with my learned friend Mr Sharp,
initial P., who is via link in Sydney, for Mr Turnbull AC.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks, Mr Horton.
MR ANDREATIDIS: Andreatidis. I appear with Ms Slack KE. We are instructed by King & Wood
Mallesons, and we are for Mr McNamara.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Have you got exhibits you want to tender, Mr Greggery?
MR GREGGERY: I do, Commissioner. I will deal with the first two witnesses only, and there is
one minor amendment. I tender exhibits numbered 67716 to 6755, but not 6721 or 6722 in
respect of which the tender is deferred.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. So that was, sorry, 67 - - -
MR GREGGERY: 16 to 6755.
COMMISSIONER: No, no. The ones you are not tendering, sorry.
MR GREGGERY: Sorry. 6721, 6722. They re-appear in the list in respect of documents related
to Mr McNamara, but Mr Scott is aware of the position.
<EXHIBITS 6716 TO 6755, EXCLUDING 6721 AND 6722, TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thanks. And you are calling Mr Turnbull?
MR GREGGERY: Yes, the next witness is the Honourable Malcolm Turnbull AC.
COMMISSIONER: Mr Turnbull, will you take an oath or an affirmation?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I will take an oath, Commissioner.

COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you. That's coming to you now. I might get you to stand even
though you're a long way away. On second thoughts, I can't see you when you stand, so
please sit.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Okay. Thank you.
<MALCOLM BLIGH TURNBULL, SWORN
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. Mr Turnbull, can you tell the Commission your full
name, please?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Malcolm Bligh Turnbull.
MR GREGGERY: Mr Turnbull, you were served with a Notice to Give a Statement and Produce
Documents marked NTG-0191 dated 10 February 2023, and you produced a signed
Statement in response dated 20 February 2023. Is that correct?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: That's true.
MR GREGGERY: And are the contents of that Statement true and correct?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. As you indicate in your Statement, Mr Turnbull, from 15
September 2015 through to 24 August 2018 you were the Prime Minister of the
Commonwealth of Australia?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And insofar as this Commission is concerned, during that period of time,
aspects of what is now known as the Robodebt Scheme were implemented or continued?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. Before we come to the specifics of your Statement, Mr Turnbull, is it
the case that in response to the Notice which required production of documents and
communications relevant to the questions, you were able to produce WhatsApp messages
communicated between yourself and then Minister Tudge and then Minister Porter and also
one of your advisers, Ms Pinkstone - Mr Pinkstone.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes, that's true. And they are in the Statement.

THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. Yes, I have.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. In terms of the manner in which you as Prime Minister interacted
with Cabinet Ministers during the period which you held office as Prime Minister, can you
describe the extent to which Ministers, as opposed to the Cabinet, were responsible for the
day-to-day functionings of their Department?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well, I ran, and committed to run, when I became Prime
Minister a traditional Cabinet government. The government was not run out of the Prime
Minister's Office as some other Prime Ministers have sought to do. I was very clear that I
expected Ministers to take responsibility for their Departments and portfolios, and for
decision-making by the government to be collegiate and run through the Cabinet process. So
when I became PM, I appointed Arthur Sinodinos, a very experienced public servant, former
Chief of Staff, of course, to John Howard, as Cabinet Secretary with the goal of restoring
traditional Cabinet government.
MR GREGGERY: And did that style or that approach inform communications that you had
with Minister Tudge and Minister Porter during 2017, for example?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes, it did.
MR GREGGERY: The role of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, as it relates to
the Department of Human Services and the Department of Social Services, did that role
include obtaining information from those Departments which were relevant to matters
which might be raised by third parties with you, such as the media or Parliament?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. The PM&C has many roles, but it's in this context its
role is really one of coordination. And so there is - there are civil servants in PM&C with
particular responsibilities, social services and health, you know, national security and so
forth. And there - they would often request information from Departments for the purpose
of briefing the Prime Minister and, of course, working with the policy advisers in my office.
MR GREGGERY: Because you were in the Prime Minister's Office, of course, you are not in a
position to say, I take it, with absolute certainty, that information conveyed from the
Department of Human Services, say, to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet was
always communicated to your office?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No, I'm not. No.
MR GREGGERY: That is, you would expect there to be some degree of filtering and briefing
where considered necessary or relevant or in response to a request by you?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes, that's - well, that's true. I mean, the - my first Chief of
Staff, a very distinguished public servant, Drew Clarke, used to say that the scarcest resource
in the Commonwealth Government is the Prime Minister's time. So managing that is, you

know, a key part of the role of the office and that - you know, that sort of informs the way in
which the interactions with PM&C are conducted.
MR GREGGERY: And I take it from your production of the WhatsApp messages, particularly
with then Ministers Tudge and Porter in the first half of 2017, none of that process precluded
you from communicating directly with your Ministers in respect of matters of public
sensitivity or the like?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No, not at all. The - there is a - there are many vectors of
engagement with Ministers, as I say in my Statement. There is the vector through the office,
through PM - and through PM&C. There is obviously the vector through Cabinet itself, but
there is also direct communications. I mean, the way a good Cabinet government operates is
in a consensual, collegiate way in which there is, you know, plenty of interaction, some of it
very formal, some of it informal. And, of course, a lot happened over WhatsApp, which is a
very convenient messaging system.
MR GREGGERY: Insofar as your approach to Cabinet - and you have referred to a more
traditional Westminster style - each year or every few years, the Department of Prime
Minister and Cabinet produced a new addition of the Cabinet Handbook for successive
ministries or governments?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes, there was. And there's also a Statement of Ministerial
Standards which is produced by - or signed off by each Prime Minister. And so - and
sometimes revised. I mean, I revised my Ministerial Standards Code after the events relating
to Barnaby Joyce, and I made a change to, you know, say that Ministers should not have
sexual relations with their staff. And I put in a lot of language in there about respect for the
Public Service and respect generally. The - but the bulk of the Ministerial Standards have
remained pretty consistent over a long period of time.
MR GREGGERY: In the successive editions of the Cabinet Handbook, the concept of Cabinet
solidarity is addressed.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes, that's right.
MR GREGGERY: And, generally speaking, requires members of Cabinet to, when speaking
publicly about Cabinet decisions, provide support for those decisions irrespective of personal
views?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes, that's - that's right.
MR GREGGERY: What in your experience as Prime Minister was the circumstance where a
question of legality was raised in respect of a Cabinet decision which was known to a Cabinet
Minister but not generally to the Cabinet? Can you speak to that circumstance?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I can't recall any circumstance of that kind. I mean, plainly
the, you know, fundamental duty of the government and Ministers is to comply with the law.

be - I mean, it would have to - it's got to be dealt with. And normally - the normal course of
action would be to get advice - get advice from the AGS and, if necessary, from the
Solicitor-General or, you know, outside counsel. But it's - and people often - as you know, as
a former lawyer, I suppose, but as lawyers know, governments are often accused of acting
ultra vires, but - sometimes correctly, sometimes not. But the fact is you have got to comply
with the law, basically. A penetrating glimpse of the obvious, you might say.
MR GREGGERY: If we turn then, to some specifics. In at least - or by at least early January
2017, there was considerable media attention in respect of the Online Compliance
Intervention program, the debt collection scheme operated by the Department of Human
Services. And at that point in time, the first week of January, Minister Tudge was on leave
overseas.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: That's true.
MR GREGGERY: I take it you were not on leave?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No - no. No, I was always on duty.
MR GREGGERY: And that led - - -
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Even if I was notionally on leave, I was always on duty.
MR GREGGERY: And that led to - that is, the media attention prompted an exchange
between yourself and Mr Tudge which commenced on about the 6th of January 2017 in
respect of that media attention?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: That's true. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Now, Mr Turnbull, I can see you have a hard copy bundle in front of you,
which I understand mirrors mine. Your Statement, of course, appears at tab 2, and I'm
referring to page 8 now.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: If you prefer an electronic copy, it's Exhibit 6724, which will undoubtedly be
shown on a screen somewhere in the room in which you are sitting.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Right.
MR GREGGERY: But at page 6 under the heading WhatsApp Messages with the Minister for
Human Services Relating to the Robodebt Scheme, your first message is recorded a little
after 11 pm, and that's a message to Mr Tudge?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.

MR GREGGERY: I see there's - there is a variance between the capitals used in his name and
that message and other messages. Is that just an autocorrect?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I assume that's a - a - I don't think - it wasn't put there by
me for emphasis, I wouldn't have thought, but I - - -
MR GREGGERY: No. Thank you.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I've just - these WhatsApps have just been, you know,
uploaded from the application so that they are exactly as they appeared.
MR GREGGERY: As they appear. Thank you. I think the - - -
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: So Alan Tudge thought the capitalised "Alan" was a subtle
way of drawing his attention to the message. That wouldn't have been a bad thing, but I
don't think that would have been my intention.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. I think page 6 is on the screen. If page 8 could be brought up.
Thank you. The passage I'm referring to, of course, is below halfway. And your first question
to him on the 6th of January was when he was back in Australia, and he indicated that the
plan was to return on 15 January, but he followed that with a tentative - with a qualification.
The next morning, you sent him a link to a news article which appeared in the Sydney
Morning Herald that day. And it was otherwise unaccompanied with any comments or
context, but the article appears behind tab 3 in - it is Exhibit 4321, an article by Peter Martin
which may have also appeared in The Canberra Times on the same date. Can I take you to
tab 4, Mr Turnbull, the second page of the document.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Mmm.
MR GREGGERY: There were two features raised by Mr Martin. The first is in the fourth
paragraph from the top commencing, "What's important.” And the second - thank you. And
the second is in the paragraph above the italicised portion towards the bottom of the page
commencing, "Many of the automated systems.” The first passage raises a question of
evidence and its relationship to the law. The second raises a question of what I might
describe as accuracy of estimates of debts according to a mathematical division process. Was
it in that context that Mr Tudge responded to you in the messages which are set out on
the - page 8 and over to page 9 of the 7th of January 2017?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well, he was - I mean, I had - you know, I don't have much
independent recollection of this exchange, you know, beyond what's in the WhatsApps. So
first - so I can't add a gloss to it. But, you know, I've - obviously I've seen the article. I've
copied it to Alan. I've - Alan Tudge. I've asked him what time zone he was in, because I
actually didn't want to, you know, disturb his slumbers if he was slumbering somewhere.
And he - and he's responded later in the day. And I was just drawing his attention to the - to
the - to the article.

MR GREGGERY: The information from Mr Tudge in his first response to you, going back to
your Statement, Exhibit 6724, page 8, identified what he described as a:
Key methodological change we made in the July 2015, which was essentially to place a
greater onus on the recipient to explain the discrepancy of data.
Beyond what is recorded there about his response to the concerns raised in the article, do
you recall him providing information to you in a telephone call or by other messages relating
to the questions of accuracy or legality generally speaking?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I don't recall the - any - the contents of any telephone calls.
But just from looking at the WhatsApp messages, it is likely that - very likely, I think, that we
were speaking and that there was an exchange that involved both telephone calls and
messaging over WhatsApp.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. The messages continue with Mr Tudge, but if I move to - sorry, I will stay
with Mr Tudge for a moment. You will see on page 9 of your Statement there is the last
message sent by you on the 8th of January 2017, which refers to speaking on with him on
Monday. Do you recall that he had indicated that he would return to Australia by the
Monday which is referred to there?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I don't recall him saying he would, but I gather he did. So he
probably did say that.
MR GREGGERY: And do you recall, insofar as you did speak with Mr Tudge from that Monday
and perhaps in the week following, whether that was in person or via telephone?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: I - I don't recall. It - I just don't recall. I think it - I've checked
my - my diary for 2017, and the - the only meeting with Mr Tudge that related to this Scheme
was not - was one with Mr Porter on the 14th of June. But I may well have spoken to him or
met with him. My diary is – was really designed - is a scheduling tool. It wasn't designed to be
a sort of ex post facto record of every encounter that I had.
MR GREGGERY: I understand. Can I take you to 13 January 2017, and that is on page 7 of
your Statement. This is a message, or a series of messages exchanged with Mr Porter, who
you may recall - - -
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Mr Porter. Right. Okay. I've got it.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Yes, Mr Porter, who you may recall was acting for Mr Tudge while
Mr Tudge was on leave.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And Mr Porter sent a relatively lengthy message to you on WhatsApp on the
13th of January, which indicated his observations in respect of what had developed over that

THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. Yes, that's right.
MR GREGGERY: The next in the sequence of events, if I take you back to your messages with
Mr Tudge, is 18 January 2017 on page 10. And the message on 18 January 2017 is from you
to Mr Tudge, commencing:
Alan, how’s it going? Got a couple of questions today about it which I hope I answered
correctly.
Pausing there, can I take you to two documents for context. The first is what appears at
paragraph 31 of your Statement on page 6.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you will see there you set out notes prepared by the relevant Minister's
Office and forwarded to your office for incorporation into your notes, and the date is 17
February 2017, that is, the day before you send the message to Mr Tudge indicating that you
had got some questions which you hoped you had answered correctly. And - sorry, I've - I've
said January when it was February. It's tab 13.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. Well, the party room meeting notes referred to in
paragraph 31 are for 17 February 2017.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: And the question about my comments to the media that are
the subject of an exchange between me and Mr Tudge are 18 January 2017, so a month
before.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. I took you to the wrong tab. I ought to have taken you to tab 13 in the
bundle, which is Exhibit 6728.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: What appears at tab 6728 is a summary of questions you were asked by
media on 17 January 2017. Commissioner, I have been provided - or, rather, I was provided
with a complete transcript of the interview, rather than just the summary, and I will tender it
as Exhibit 6728A so it can be inserted behind the summary which appears at tab 13.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Alright. It's admitted with that number.
<EXHIBIT 6728A TENDERED AND MARKED
MR GREGGERY: Yes.

COMMISSIONER: I'm not sure if I actually said before that the other exhibits were admitted,
but they are according to the schedule with the two exceptions.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. The point I was getting to, Mr Turnbull, was the question which
you raised effectively in your message to Mr Tudge on 18 January where you make the
comment, "I hope I answered correctly," does that reflect the general process whereby your
speaking notes rely upon material produced by the Department of Human Services?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well, yes, I think - yes. Well, let me explain. The - the Brief
that I had in January on the way the Scheme was operating was informed by brief speaking
notes, if you like, that were given to me - or given to my office by the Minister - relevant
Ministers, in this case Mr Tudge's office. So, yes, we were briefed by them. But as - you
know, I didn't read - I mean, the context, Commissioner, was a press conference at the CPO
in Sydney on the 18th of January in which I was announcing changes to the Ministry. And
then the press conference ensued and then there was a question relating to the - what was
called the Centrelink Robo letters, which I answered, and some of that answer is in the press
report. But I just draw your attention to - to this point. I say at the end:
Obviously it is important to make sure that the recipient gets the letter, and you've seen the
measures that the Minister Alan Tudge has announced.
So I was referencing the changes, you know, which is - which is referred to in the WhatsApps
of having the initial letter going out by registered post so that - so that the Centrelink or the
Department actually knew whether the people had got the letter or not.
COMMISSIONER: Did you have much confidence Mr Tudge actually had a good grasp on
what this system entailed?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well - look, I had - Alan Tudge I - I always regarded as a
technocrat. You know, he had - he had - he was a management consultant. He had a lot of
experience. I didn't - I didn't regard him as being a negligent or incompetent or careless
Minister, but I did - there is a - a WhatsApp here where you can see on the 20th of January
2017 where I say:
Alan, we need a frank assessment of what the problems are and what is happening to fix
them. Are you sure your Department is giving you the right advice on what is happening?
So, you know, I - I guess I was pressing him, Commissioner, to do his job. That was - you
know, that was what I was seeking to do. And he gave - - -
COMMISSIONER: On the 7th of January - - -
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Sorry.
COMMISSIONER: I'm sorry. You go.

COMMISSIONER: On 7th of January, he had assured you that it wasn't correct to say that
they were simply taking the average of the income declared to ATO and applying it evenly
across 26 fortnights. But as must have become apparent to you at some stage, that's exactly
what happened in many cases.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Look, I - I don't - I just don't recall that, I'm afraid. I
was - yes, my recollection is pretty much limited to what we have - what I have in the
Statement.
COMMISSIONER: And so you were oblivious to the fact that he had confidently declared no
recovery fee was being charged and, in fact, it was?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well, I accepted him on - I accepted what he was saying as,
you know, he was the responsible Minister. So - - -
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: So - I mean, having said that, Commissioner - look, these
WhatsApps are part of a larger universe of communication between - most of which went on
between my office - the policy adviser in my office and PM&C, and they - the WhatsApps, if
you like, represent the direct - just the direct communication between me and the Ministers.
But, you know, as you can see from the record, I - I was, you know, obviously talking a lot and
communicating on WhatsApp also with my policy adviser, Kerry Pinkstone, and, you know, if
you like, tick-tacking with her about what she was doing and what she was learning.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. It is a bit surprising, though, that he had made that statement to you
that the averaging wasn't happening, effectively, and it must have become apparent to you
at some stage that it was, that you wouldn't find that a bit unsettling.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well, I - look, I don't - I don't recall - I don't recall being
unsettled by that, but I - you know, I may have - I may have been. I'm sorry, I just don't have
a - I don't have an independent recollection of this episode beyond the material that I've
produced.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Mr Turnbull, can I take you to tab 4, Exhibit 4684. It was not a
communication - or is not a communication to which you were a party. It's 7 February 2017.
But it refers to what - that is, it's a communication within persons in the Department of
Human Services, but it refers to information provided to the Department of Prime Minister
and Cabinet on 7 January, that is, a month earlier. And the third paragraph commencing,
"The methodology," is the relevant one. It asserts, firstly, that:
The method for assessing and calculating a debt has not changed, and averaging is only used
where the customer does not provide the detailed information.

And continues. Do you have any recollection of being informed about that fact in early
January?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No, I - I mean, I have very little recollection independent of
the documentary materials that I've produced.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. Thank you. And if I move, then, to the 3rd of March, Exhibit 3671. It's
behind tab 16, Mr Turnbull.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. This was a letter - or is a letter sent by Mr Tudge and Mr Porter
to you. It is dated on the third page, .0947, 3 March 2017. It refers to various aspects of the
automated system. And on the first page in the paragraph under the redaction, it refers to:
The targeting of compliance actions for certain Centrelink recipients… The anomalies
identified in Australian Taxation Office and Department of Human Services data sets.
But doesn't specifically refer to the way in which those anomalies were used to allege debts.
Do you recall beyond what is put in this letter - and I appreciate the answer you just
gave - whether in any meetings with Mr Tudge and Mr Porter in March or subsequently
referred especially to the question of averaging?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No, I do not recall that. I - as I've said in my Statement, I
have no doubt this letter was shown to me, and I would have read it when it was shown to
me - or given to me. But I don't - I don't recall it today.
MR GREGGERY: Can I take you to page 3 of the document, Mr Turnbull.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: At the first paragraph, there is a reference to Data61 at the CSIRO and the
Digital Transformation Agency. At least one of your WhatsApp messages, I think, to Mr Tudge
referred to the Digital Transformation Agency. Do you recall prompting Mr Tudge or
Mr Tudge and Mr Porter to - towards having someone outside of the Department look at the
process or the Scheme generally?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. I certainly referred - recommended them to talk to the
DTA, the Digital Transformation Agency. I gather Mr Tudge said in his evidence to the
Commission that I also encouraged them to talk to Data61. I don't recall doing so, but it
would have been consistent with the approach I had. I mean, I had a - I established - I was
involved in - actually in the - in the restructuring of the entity that became Data61, but I
actually established DTA, you know, from de novo, if you like, when I was Communications
Minister. So I had a strong interest in that area, and I also believed that government should
be providing these type - you know, sourcing these sort of digital - this sort of digital
expertise in-house rather than constantly going out to consultants and, you know, develop

definitely recommended the DTA. It's in the WhatsApp. I may well have recommended
Data61 as well. That - they have got complementary capabilities, I would say. They overlap.
They do different things.
MR GREGGERY: And if I can take you to the last paragraph on that page.
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: It is the dot point which commences, "We will pursue.” It refers to the
engagement of PricewaterhouseCoopers. Pausing there, PwC falls into that category of
external consultant, that is, outside the government to which you just referred, I think,
between - - -
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Yes. Yes. I mean, I'm not - look, I've got nothing against
PricewaterhouseCoopers or consultants, you know, per se. But the - there is a - this is way - I
think - I suspect, way beyond your area of interest, but there is a problem which I sought to
address in government with what are actually core responsibilities of government, the Public
Service, being outsourced to consultants, which has the consequence of effectively deskilling
the Public Service. I mean, that was why I set up an inquiry into the Public Service which
David Thodey chaired, you know, to really - that was one of the issues we were seeking to
address. So it is a - you know, consultants have their place, but you've got to make sure
you've got a strong skill base in your APS.
MR GREGGERY: Do you recall ever being briefed in respect of information generated by PwC
in respect of the Scheme through 2017?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No. No, I do not.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. You refer in your Statement to, I think, a general awareness, but
correct me if I have misunderstood, that the - the Online Compliance Intervention program
and its variants were line items relatively consistently in the Budget throughout successive
years. Would it have - would it be unusual if PwC addressed questions of the achievability of
Budget Measures in their consultancy engagement for - - -
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: No, I think they would - they - I don't know what the terms
of their engagement were, but they - they would - they could be called upon to give advice
on the achievability of financial targets, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And if that was the case, they did address that in their material, would it be
surprising to you for briefs of that nature to make their way to at least your office?
THE HON MALCOLM TURNBULL: Well, look, I - I mean, a lot of information comes into the
Prime Minister's Office. I simply don't know whether a brief from PricewaterhouseCoopers
did or not. But it wouldn't surprise me if it didn't. You know, the - at any given time,
Government Departments are getting, you know, enormous amount of consulting work
done, and advice given. You can't all be shovelled into the Prime Minister's Office.

MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. No further questions.
